title: A Town Built for a Feeling
logline: A town laid out on a cold plain at six thousand feet in the tropics, so that people could have the exact sensations of somewhere else delivered to them at altitude, filmed in the weather it was built for, which is the one thing nobody could ship, keep or own.
human_question: If you could arrange to be touched by one feeling on demand, for the rest of your life, what would you build, and what would be left standing once the feeling stopped coming?

place.what_kind_of_place: A hill town and district capital at about 1,870 metres, on a level plain two miles long ringed by mountains, and still laid out the way it was planned in the middle of the nineteenth century: a public garden with gravel walks and flowerbeds, a racecourse on the flat of the valley with a grandstand down one side, golf links whose fairways run up into the hills, a dammed lake made out of a river, clipped hedges along the walls, brick and half-timbered buildings with working chimneys in them, and hill streams stocked a century ago with a fish that was not here before. The mean annual temperature is sixteen degrees, the mean night minimum stays between ten and fourteen all year, frost is recorded in the coldest weeks, the record low is minus two point six, and in July the place receives about a fifth of the sunshine it could theoretically get. It is also, and mainly, a working town in its own right, of some tens of thousands of people, with a municipal council, a market, a bus stand, dairies, a vegetable trade, hotels, schools and a hospital, whose residents live in the cold the way anybody lives in their own weather.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because the thing this town exists for is one of the very few interior states a camera can photograph directly: temperature. Breath. Rain standing in beads on the tips of mown grass. A hedge dripping in a line. Condensation running down the inside of a windowpane with a street out of focus behind it. Low cloud coming across a racecourse at the height of a standing person, so that the far rail is there, then gone, then there. Wool, steam, a fire lit in the middle of the afternoon. And the light itself: flat, sourceless, grey, with no shadow anywhere in the frame, which is the exact opposite of every other film in this group. The strongest frame the place offers is also its plainest, a wide wet expanse of imported grass with cloud crossing it, and that frame is the argument.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing except the air, and nothing at all that the crew arranges. Cloud arrives at ground level and leaves. Drizzle starts, stops and starts. A window fogs and clears. Once a year, for a few weeks in April, the whole town fills up, the races are run, the flower show goes up under canvas and every room is taken, and then it empties again and the cloud has the place to itself for the rest of the year. The camera mostly does not move. Where the other films in this group are carried by work and hands, this one is carried by weather crossing a fixed frame.
place.when_it_looks_best: The overcast months, May to September, when recorded sunshine falls to between a fifth and a quarter of the possible and mean humidity sits at eighty-five to eighty-seven per cent. July is the extreme of it. Early morning and the hour before dark for cloud at ground level; January and February for the coldest nights, breath and any chance of frost, at the cost of brighter days. Explicitly not sunset and explicitly not golden hour: there is no warm light anywhere in this film, and the payoff is weather rather than light. A clear blue day is a wasted day here, which is the reverse of the usual rule.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A cold, quiet, almost still film about a town that looks as though it were assembled somewhere else and set down in the tropics, watched in the weather it was made for. Mist on a racecourse, wet grass, hedges, chimneys, breath, a fire in the afternoon, a bus with fogged windows, then the town crammed and loud for a few weeks in April and empty again. It has a complete shape of its own without a word of narration: the cloud comes down, the place goes into it, the cloud lifts and the place is still there. For a viewer who wants nothing but beautiful footage it is the coolest, softest, stillest thing in the series, and the only one where the payoff is a temperature.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes an unusually literal demonstration. The books this series draws on keep a list of the ordinary occasions on which wanting shows up, and the list turns out to name, item by item, most of what is in frame: preparing pleasing things, among them houses, and then using them; looking at beautiful things for the pleasure of looking; playing games and watching them; music, scent, good food; and journeys taken for pleasure. Here a whole town is that item, built at altitude so that a particular set of contacts would be available on demand. Then the voice does the harder half. The same books say that arranging things to keep the cold off, or out of a plain sense of what is useful, is not counted a fault at all, and they count momentary states of mind rather than people, centuries or places. So the film records what was carried up here and refuses to rule on the mind that carried it, and ends on the one thing the apparatus could never hold: the weather it was built for, which arrives on its own schedule, crosses the grass and goes.

sequence.on_screen: Flat grey light, nothing identifiable yet. Long lens on a tripod, locked off: a wide expanse of short mown grass, soaked, with low cloud moving across it at about the height of a standing person. A white painted rail comes out of the cloud and goes back into it. No people, no movement but the cloud.
sequence.voice: This is the tropics, six thousand feet up, and it is sixteen degrees and raining. None of what you are looking at grew here. The grass was sown. The trees along the edge of it were carried up as seedlings. So were the hedges. So were the fish in the stream at the bottom of the hill. Somebody wanted a particular set of sensations, and rather than travel to them, had them brought up the mountain.

sequence.on_screen: The town in the same light, one static frame each, no camera movement: shutters going up, a bus with its windows fogged from the inside, steam standing off a glass of tea, breath, brick and half-timber and a chimney with smoke in it, a clipped hedge running along a wall, a wet road with no shadow on it.
sequence.voice: A man named Samuel Baker, then in his mid-twenties, came up here in 1847, sent to the hill station to get over a fever, and got better in a fortnight. He found about twenty houses, a barracks for invalid soldiers, an inn he described as the perfection of everything dirty, and a bazaar where two hundred people already lived. He went home, bought land, and came back the next year with nine emigrants and a blacksmith, a bull, a shorthorn cow, three rams, a horse and a pack of hounds. The cow weighed thirteen hundredweight, the van built to carry her collapsed under her, and she walked the hundred and fifteen miles up, ten miles a day.

sequence.on_screen: The apparatus, one long held frame each, all of it in overcast and all of it nearly empty: the flat oval of the racecourse and its grandstand with nobody in it; the public garden's gravel walks, mown lawns and flowerbeds; the mown greens of the links running up into cloud; the dammed lake with the far bank missing; a stream with fly-fishing water in it.
sequence.voice: Then it was assembled, piece by dated piece. A governor dammed the stream in 1873 and a bog became the lake. The first race meeting was run in 1875. Trout went into the water in 1881, put there by an official whose name is on the record, so that there would be a fish here to catch. A soldier laid out the golf course in 1889. And the first tree planted in the public garden was an oak. The books this film is about keep a list of the ordinary occasions when wanting turns up, and the list is oddly specific. Looking at beautiful things for the pleasure of looking. Playing games. Watching them. Preparing pleasing things, among them houses, and then using them. Journeys taken for pleasure.

sequence.on_screen: Close and static, long lens: rain standing in beads along the tips of the grass. A hedge dripping. Condensation running down the inside of a windowpane. A wood fire lit in a grate in the middle of the afternoon. A hand round a cup with steam coming off it.
sequence.voice: What these books are counting is not a town and not a lifetime. They are counting moments, and the moment they mean is a meeting: a mind and something agreeable arriving at the same instant, and a small movement towards it. They have a term for the quality a thing carries when it is met that way. They call it the taste of the object. A town cannot want anything. What a town can do is make the meeting happen on schedule.

sequence.on_screen: People in the town going about the cold, all filmed wide and from a distance, nobody singled out: a bus queue under umbrellas, a coat being buttoned, a woollen hat pulled down, a shopkeeper's heater, a shawl, wet paving, someone sweeping standing water off a step.
sequence.voice: And here the books stop and refuse to help. The same arranging, they say, done to keep the cold off, or out of a plain sense of what is useful, is not counted a fault at all. So nothing in this valley can be read off its surface. A hedge is a hedge either way. The record is exact about what was brought up here and by whom, and it says nothing whatever about the mind that brought it. No photograph of any of it ever will.

sequence.on_screen: The same frames twice. April: every room taken, cars nose to tail on the lake road, the garden full, the racecourse crowded and loud, a flower show going up under canvas. Then the identical set-ups in July: empty verges, shuttered fronts, the grandstand used as shelter from a shower, cloud where the far side of the course was.
sequence.voice: Once a year the town fills. A guidebook from a hundred years ago says the same thing in almost the same words, that everybody came up for the races and every bungalow, hotel and club was taxed to its utmost. Journeys taken for pleasure are on that list too, written down centuries before anybody drove up here for a long weekend. Then the season ends. Most of the year, this is what the place is.

sequence.on_screen: The town at its own business in the same weather, and nobody in frame held long enough to be read: the market under plastic sheeting, milk cans on a step, a van unloading, a barber's lit window, two people walking the lake path, a dog under a bench, work going on in drizzle, and the ground floor of the grandstand.
sequence.voice: This is somebody's town. People were born here, work here, will die here, and the cold is simply where they live. When there was no racing, the public library was kept on the ground floor of the grandstand; racing stopped altogether for twenty-five years and then started again. The books make one more distinction that matters to a camera: the same reaching arrives with delight in one person and as flat routine in another, and never with displeasure. So a face is not evidence of anything. And of the fifty-four kinds of everyday mind they count, twenty-four are called beautiful. They are not writing off the ordinary world, and they are not writing off anybody standing in it.

sequence.on_screen: The payoff, held far longer than is comfortable: the wet empty expanse of imported grass with cloud moving across it, the far rail appearing and disappearing, light flat and without a single shadow in the frame. No sun comes out. Cut to black while it is still happening.
sequence.voice: Everything that was carried up here is still here. The grass, the rails, the chimneys, the hedges, the fish. The one thing it was all built for cannot be carried, cannot be kept and cannot be owned by anybody. It arrives on its own schedule, crosses the grass, and goes. It is doing it now, whether or not anyone came up the mountain to feel it.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, C004 supplies the arena and C005 supplies the occasions, and this town is where the two become one object. C004's Margaya defines greed as the attaching that takes things and persons to be good, beautiful or sweet [C004-M:L13], and then does something the other digests do not: it says every object carries one of three qualities and calls that quality the taste of the object, and that a greed-rooted mind arises together with the experiencing of the good or the middling taste and never with displeasure [C004-M:L15]. The Pradeepika puts the same thing as an event rather than a state: when a mind meets an agreeable or neutral object of form or sound, a sticking to it arises [C004-P:L41], inside a count of the minds that belong to the world of sense experience [C004-P:L25]. So the occasion is a meeting, and a meeting needs the object to be present. C005's Margaya then lists where such meetings ordinarily happen, and the list reads like an inventory of this valley: looking at beautiful things for the pleasure of it, playing games, watching games, preparing pleasing objects among which it names houses, and using them [C005-M:L5], with journeys taken for pleasure added in the following line [C005-M:L7]. A town planted at altitude to guarantee a particular set of contacts is not an analogy for that list; it is that list, built.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: Two things neither concept gives alone. First, prompting. The Margaya divides these minds by whether they arise on their own or through a prompting, and says the prompting may come from others or from oneself [C004-M:L21]. A built town is a prompt with nobody left in it: hedges, rails, mown grass and a grandstand are a standing arrangement for contact, maintained for a century and three quarters after everyone who wanted it had gone. The apparatus outlasts the moment it was built to produce, and the sources are counting the moment, not the apparatus. Second, the refusal. C005 draws its line by aim and not by act: the same arranging done from faith, from kindness, or with a plain regard for usefulness is not counted unwholesome [C005-M:L9], and it says outright that clothing prepared and worn in order to remove the cold is not a fault [C005-M:L17]. This town's whole subject is cold. So the concept that looks as though it will convict the place is the same concept that forbids the conviction, and the film ends where the books end, with an object fully described and a mind not available for inspection. That is why the payoff is weather: the one item in the inventory that could not be shipped, stocked or fenced, and that arrives whether or not anybody is there to meet it.

concept_links.why: The film is built on the Margaya's own list of everyday occasions, which names looking at beautiful things for the pleasure of looking, playing and watching games, preparing pleasing objects including houses, and consuming them [C005-M:L5], and then journeys taken for pleasure [C005-M:L7]. A town laid out to deliver a chosen set of sensations is that list at the scale of a valley, which is why the location carries the concept without analogy. Four limits from the digest are load-bearing and sit in the sequence rather than only in the risks. First, this is not an only-intentions teaching: the same source still names theft, lying, divisive speech and misconduct as courses of harm carried out through wanting [C005-M:L3], so nothing here licenses a reading in which what was done does not matter. Second, the aim is what counts and the aim is not visible: the same arranging done from faith, kindness or a regard for usefulness is not unwholesome [C005-M:L9], and beat five is that sentence. Third, the source does not preach deprivation: it allows wealth earned and spent with discernment [C005-M:L9] and even valuable clothes worn to escape contempt [C005-M:L19], the latter flagged in the digest for expert check and therefore not used in the voice. Fourth, and specific to a cold film, the source explicitly exempts arranging things in order to remove cold [C005-M:L17], which is the one sentence that stops this becoming a sermon against people who wanted to be warm or cool. The claim that most of an ordinary day runs on such minds [C005-M:L7] is the author's unquantified general statement and is not voiced at all here, because on a colonial subject it would read as a verdict on a community rather than a remark about minds. Finally, the digest's does_not_transfer lines are applied directly: it forbids framing devoted family life as greedy, reading the source as only-intentions-matter, preaching minimalism, and implying that art, music, sport or games are sinful, and since this film carries games, a racecourse, a golf links, music and a flower show, the last of those is the live one. The voice never says the sports are a fault, only that the books list them among the occasions where wanting turns up.

C004 keeps the fault off the town and off everybody in it. Greed is defined as the attaching, not as the thing attached to [C004-M:L13], so a film made almost entirely of a pleasant place cannot become a warning about pleasant places. The digest's account of the object is what gives the film its central image: every object carries a good, bad or middling quality, that quality is called the taste of the object, and the greed-rooted mind arises together with the experiencing of it and never with displeasure [C004-M:L15], while the Pradeepika makes the occasion a meeting between a mind and an agreeable object of form or sound [C004-P:L41]. That is why a town is describable as an apparatus for producing contact of a chosen kind, and why the ending has to be weather: a meeting cannot be stockpiled. Three guards come straight from the digest. The same reaching comes with joy in one person and with a flat neutral feeling in another [C004-M:L17], so no face in frame is evidence and beat seven says so out loud. Twenty-four of the fifty-four minds in this count are called beautiful and the sense world is not treated as a trap [C004-P:L27], so the film is not entitled to imply that ordinary enjoyment is a failing. And the Pradeepika's own stretch of contemporary moral commentary [C004-P:L55-L69] is flagged by the digest as the author's argument, not the teaching, and as something that would wound if turned into a judgment on a community; on a colonial subject that warning is the whole discipline of this film, which records and does not adjudicate. Two digest uncertainties are respected by omission: the same line's listing of affection and love among the names of greed [C004-M:L13] is flagged for expert check and is not used, and the account of the first mental process after conception [C004-P:L73] is not used either. Of the digest's does_not_transfer lines, two are the ones this film could break: turning the author's social commentary into a judgment on people or communities, and calling the sense world a trap. Beats five and seven exist to hold them.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That an occasion of wanting is a meeting between a mind and something agreeable, that it lasts as long as the meeting and no longer, and that you can therefore build a very large and very permanent thing in order to arrange a very small and very temporary one. And that the arrangement records nothing about the mind that made it: the same hedge, the same grass, the same fire in the afternoon serve need and serve pleasure identically, which is why the books sort by aim and a camera cannot.
what_must_be_real: The weather. Every frame of cloud, drizzle, breath, standing water and flat light is filmed as it occurs, never simulated, never composited, never graded into being, and the film waits for the weather rather than shooting whatever the week offers. No frost or mist is faked or enhanced. The town is filmed as a working town: nobody is directed, nobody is asked to walk again, no shopkeeper is asked to light a heater for the camera and no fire is lit for a shot. No identifiable resident, worker or visitor is framed as wanting anything, and nobody is asked why they came, what they paid or what they were hoping for. No interior of a club, hotel or private house is filmed in a way that turns living people into period dressing. The historical claims in the voice are held to what the primary record actually says: Baker's own book is the authority for the 1847 visit, the state of the station he found, the two hundred people already living in the bazaar, the emigrants and the animals, and if any of it fails checking against the printed text it comes out of the voice rather than being softened. The much-quoted phrase about importing the appurtenances of a country town is not in his book and is not put in his mouth. Hunting, which is in the record of the station's pastimes, is not filmed, not narrated and not illustrated.
position_hint: late middle: the group's cold film and its only town, best placed after the films in which one person reaches for one thing, because it is the point where the reaching stops being a gesture and becomes a permanent installation somebody else has to live in. It also works as the group's held breath before wanting meets a wall, since its ending is not a refusal but an indifference. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Nostalgia. This is the single biggest risk and it is built into the location: the whole tourist vocabulary of the place is charm, quaintness and a lost era, and one soft shot of a fireplace or one wistful line of narration would turn the film into the postcard it exists to refuse. The film is not admiring the imitation and is not sneering at it either, and neither the voice nor the grade may imply that anything here was better before.
The nickname. The place's famous two-word nickname is a place name and a tourist cliche, and it appears nowhere in the prose, the voice or a caption.

Adjudicating colonial history. The record is recorded and never judged, in either direction. No denunciation, no defence, no irony in the voice. The plantation economy and its labour history are real, are not this film's subject, and are not gestured at decoratively or used as a moral background; nobody's hardship is narrated.

Turning residents into set dressing in somebody else's fantasy, or into a contrast with the colonists. People in this town are in their own town. Nobody is framed as acquisitive and nobody is an object of judgement, which is this group's specific problem stated plainly: a camera cannot show greed [C004-M:L17].
Narrating anybody's class or ethnicity, past or present. The film does not, and the record's demographic detail stays out of the voice entirely.

Animal killing as spectacle. Hunting and angling are in the documentary record of the station and the film keeps them to the bare fact that a fish was introduced. No shooting, no hooking, no landed fish, no gravestone of a famous hunter.
Preaching against pleasure, sport or a holiday, when the source allows wealth spent with discernment and does not condemn games or music [C005-M:L9].
Implying that wanting to be cold or warm is itself the fault, when the source explicitly exempts arranging things to remove cold [C005-M:L17].
Reading the sources as only-intentions-matter, when the same passage names particular acts as courses of harm [C005-M:L3].

Style collision inside the district. Five other films on the slate sit in this district and one of them, in another group, is built on cloud on a mountain reserve. This film's cloud is only ever over mown grass, hedges, rails and roofs; no wilderness, no summit, no waterfall, no power station, no vegetable collecting point and no tea estate appears in it, and the archetypes already used up include tea estates, railways and hydro.
Golden hour creeping back in. The payoff is a temperature, not a light, and a warm sunset over the lake would be the easiest and worst shot available here.

Weather dependence. The whole film rests on obtaining low cloud, drizzle and flat light, which are common in the named months but not orderable; and the April material for beat six has to be shot in a different season from everything else, which means two trips at minimum.

Drone permission and airspace over a municipality and a lake used as a waterdrome are unverified and may be refused; the treatment is deliberately written so that the film survives with no drone at all.
drop_if: The weather cannot be obtained: if a schedule cannot be held long enough to film cloud at ground level over the grass, the film has no payoff and should not be made.
Filming the racecourse, the garden or the links is only possible as an event shoot with participants and crowds as the subject, which would make people the exhibit.
The only access to the interiors and the historic buildings is on terms that require them to be shown as charming period pieces.
The history cannot be held to the primary record, leaving the voice resting on the guidebook version of a founder who imported a country town wholesale.

connections.note: One film climbs for a taste that only exists where it grows; this one shows a whole town built so that a set of sensations would not have to be travelled to at all.

Both films turn on weather, and they must not be shot alike: there weather is what a crop tastes of, in heat and bright light; here weather is the object somebody built a town to obtain, in flat grey and stillness.

selection.reason: The group's cold film and its only town, and the one place where the occasions of wanting can be shown as a permanent built installation rather than as a hand reaching for something.

review.note: Replaced entirely, location and all, and the earlier verdict is therefore void. The previous film was a dry-zone reservoir where lotus buds are picked from inner tubes before dawn, and it was one of fourteen candidates in this group that were all working places, markets or trades with no historical story running between them; Chathura ruled that a group cannot be a monoculture, and this is one of five replacements. This record is now the group's cold film and its only town: a planted hill station at about 1,870 metres, filmed in overcast, drizzle and low cloud, with no golden hour anywhere in it, a payoff that is a wet empty expanse of imported grass with cloud crossing it rather than a light or a reveal, and almost no camera movement, which is a treatment no other film in the group uses. It is bound to a documented history rather than to an analogy: a governor built a stone house and barracks for invalid soldiers here in 1828 because the climate was treated as medicine; Samuel Baker arrived as one of those invalids in 1847, recovered in a fortnight, and came back in 1848 with nine emigrants, a blacksmith, seeds, saw-mills, a bull, a shorthorn cow that walked a hundred and fifteen miles because the van built for her collapsed, three rams, a thoroughbred horse and a pack of hounds, hoping in his own words to establish a little village around his residence; his brother brought horse racing; a governor dammed a stream in 1873 and made the lake; the first race meeting was run in 1875 and the present course laid out in 1900; trout were put into the lake in 1881 by a named official; a soldier laid out the golf course in 1889; and the first tree planted in the public garden was an oak. By 1908 a guidebook could list the whole apparatus from the mountain above it, and its list matches the Margaya's list of everyday occasions almost item for item. Both concept links were re-tested against their digests and rewritten: C005 is re-grounded on the occasions line that names the preparing and using of pleasing objects including houses, on the aim line that exempts the same arranging done from usefulness, and above all on the line that exempts arranging things in order to remove cold, which is what stops a cold film becoming a sermon; C004 is re-grounded on the definition that keeps the fault off the object, on the taste of the object and the meeting that produces it, on prompting that may come from others or from oneself, which is what a built town is, and on joy-or-flat feeling as the reason no face is evidence. The digest's warning about the Pradeepika's own social commentary is treated as the film's governing discipline: the colonial record is recorded and never adjudicated, there is no denunciation and no defence, the plantation labour history is not used as background, the place's famous nickname never appears because it is a place name, hunting is kept to a bare factual mention and never filmed, and nobody living in the town is framed as acquisitive or as anybody's contrast. Place, two_layers, an eight-beat sequence, a full historical_thread from Baker's own book and a 1908 guidebook read directly, seven verified Commons images and a new location record were written from scratch. New title, with the old title kept in aliases. Connections re-pointed inside the group, including an explicit instruction that this film and the group's other weather film must not be shot alike.

suggested_location.name: Nuwara Eliya town

also_known_as.name: Nuwara Eliya
also_known_as.meaning: commonly glossed as the city on the plain or table land, and also as the city of light

also_known_as.name: Newera Ellia
also_known_as.meaning: the nineteenth-century English spelling used throughout Samuel Baker's own book

suggested_location.region: Nuwara Eliya town and its plain, Nuwara Eliya District, Central Province: the district capital, on the level valley below Pidurutalagala
suggested_location.why_here: It is the only place on the slate where a whole settlement is the object the concept describes, and where the thing it was built to deliver is something a camera can photograph directly. The record is unusually complete and unusually literal: a governor built a stone house here in 1828 and barracks for invalid soldiers, because the climate was treated as medicine; a young invalid named Samuel Baker came up in 1847, recovered in a fortnight, went home and came back the next year with nine emigrants, a blacksmith, seeds, saw-mills, a bull, a shorthorn cow, three rams, a thoroughbred horse and a pack of hounds, hoping, in his own words, to establish a little village around his own residence and to make a life here something approaching a country life at home; his brother is credited with bringing horse racing; a governor dammed a stream in 1873 and made the lake out of a bog; trout went into that lake in 1881; a soldier laid out the golf course in 1889; the first race meeting was run in 1875 and the present course in 1900; and the first tree planted in the public garden, formally named in 1897, was an oak. By 1908 a guidebook could stand on the mountain above and list what was on the plain: two lakes, a racecourse, two golf links, clubs with their recreation grounds, a well-stocked trout stream and a public garden. That is C005's list of occasions, built. And the sensation the whole apparatus was for is weather: a mean of sixteen degrees, night minima of ten to fourteen, frost in the coldest weeks, and in July about a fifth of the possible sunshine, which is why this is the group's cold film and why the payoff is a wet empty expanse of imported grass with cloud crossing it rather than any kind of light. It is also, and this is the reason the film is possible at all without condescension, a working district capital where tens of thousands of people live, whose grandstand housed the town library outside the racing season, and whose racecourse was shut for twenty-five years and reopened. Five other films on the slate are in this district and none is a town: they are a reservoir drawdown, a waterfall and headworks, a power station, a nature reserve and a vegetable-collecting village. No monument, no working trade, no crowd, no heat and no golden hour.

historical_thread.story:
The plain was not empty when it was planted, and the man usually named as the town's founder did not find it empty.

The station existed first as medicine. Sir Edward Barnes, fifth Governor of Ceylon, opened the road up to the plain and on for thirty-six miles beyond it, and in 1828 built himself a single-storey holiday residence there, Barnes Hall, at a reported cost of eight thousand pounds; the building is now the town's grand hotel, rebuilt and enlarged. Samuel Baker, writing of what he found twenty years later, credits Barnes with the whole existence of the sanatorium: 'To him alone indeed are we indebted for the existence of a sanitarium. It was he who opened the road... At his own expense he built a substantial mansion at a cost, as it is said, of eight thousand pounds, and with provident care for the health of the European troops, he erected barracks and officers' quarters for the invalids.' Convalescents were sent up because the air was believed to cure them.

Baker came up in 1847 as one of them, ordered to the highlands by his doctor after a year of shooting trips and a severe attack of jungle fever. He was there a fortnight. His own account of the arrival is the most useful thing in the record, because it describes the sensation and the place in the same breath: 'But the climate! what can I say to describe the wonderful effects of such a pure and unpolluted air? Simply, that at the expiration of a fortnight, in spite of the tough beef, and the black bread and potatoes, I was as well and as strong as I ever had been.' He is equally plain about the station: the rest-house was 'the perfection of everything that was dirty and uncomfortable', the place 'a land of starvation' and 'the most miserable place conceivable'. And he counts it: 'The station then consisted of about twenty private residences, the barracks and officers' quarters, the resthouse and the bazaar; the latter containing about two hundred native inhabitants.' Two hundred people were already living on this plain before any of the apparatus existed.

What he wanted is stated without any ambiguity at all. He went home, and returned as a settler, hoping 'to effect such a change in the rough face of Nature in that locality as to render a residence at Newera Ellia something approaching to a country life in England, with the advantage of the whole of Ceylon for my manor, and no expense of gamekeepers', and 'sanguinely looking forward to establishing a little English village around my own residence'. He bought land from the government at twenty shillings an acre. He engaged a bailiff, who came with his wife and daughter and nine other emigrants including a blacksmith. He bought 'farming implements of the most improved descriptions, seeds of all kinds, saw-mills, etc., etc., and the following stock: A half-bred bull (Durham and Hereford), a well-bred Durham cow, three rams (a Southdown, Leicester and Cotswold), and a thorough-bred entire horse by Charles XII.; also a small pack of foxhounds and a favorite greyhound ("Bran").' The party sailed from London in the Earl of Hardwick in September 1848, Baker having gone ahead by the overland mail in August. The shorthorn cow weighed about thirteen hundredweight and was too fat to march: a van was built for her which the maker said would carry an elephant, and it collapsed under her at the first attempt, so she walked the hundred and fifteen miles up from the coast with the bull, the sheep, the horse and the hounds, at ten miles a day. Baker's own settlement was not the town: he chose a site about two and a half miles away, at the eastern end of the plain, where the ground was level enough for a plough.

He arrived to build in October, in the south-west monsoon, and left the best description of this film's weather that exists: 'the mist boiled up from the valleys and swept along the surface of the plains, obscuring the view of everything, except the pattering rain which descended without ceasing day or night. Every sound was hushed, save that of the elements and the distant murmuring roar of countless waterfalls; not a bird chirped, the dank white lichens hung from the branches of the trees, and the wretchedness of the place was beyond description.' A fortnight later the gale ceased and he wrote: 'It was like a beautiful cool mid-summer in England.'

The apparatus went up over the following half-century, and every piece of it is dated. Baker's brother John is credited with introducing horse racing, having made a training course in the 1840s on a hill near his house for imported English thoroughbreds. In 1873 Governor Sir William Gregory authorised the damming of the Thalagala stream, which runs off the mountain above the town, in order to make more land available for the town's expansion; the swampy bog at the foot of the hills became the lake. The first race meeting was held in 1875, organised by the local Gymkhana Club; meetings ran intermittently until 1900, when the present course was laid out. In 1881 the lake was stocked with trout by C. J. R. Le Mesurier, the Assistant Government Agent. In 1889 a Scottish soldier of the Gordon Highlanders laid out the golf course; it opened in 1890 with nine holes, a five-room pavilion was built overlooking the links in 1892, and it was extended to eighteen holes in 1893, covering about a hundred acres. The public garden, which had been the research field of the botanical garden down the road, was formally named in 1897 for Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, and was established with the planting of its first tree, an oak, by a visiting German princess.

By the first decade of the twentieth century H. W. Cave could survey the plain from the mountain above it and simply list the contents: 'an extensive plateau encircled by hills and possessing two lakes, a racecourse, two golf links, various clubs with their recreation grounds, a well-stocked trout stream, a lovely public garden, several good hotels, fine residences dotting the hill-sides... and for most of the year a charming climate, bright and cool as an ideal English spring.' He records that 'the lake is full of carp, and trout have been successfully introduced into the neighbouring streams, licences to fish in which are granted for any period', and that the fishing club 'has leased from the Government the fishing rights in all waters at an elevation of over five thousand feet above sea level'. On the season he is exact about the scale of the wanting: 'All Colombo flocks to Nuwara Eliya for the races... Every bungalow, hotel, and club is taxed to its utmost capacity. Many who cannot find accommodation ride daily into the station, distances of twenty and even thirty miles not being considered too great even when followed by a dance at the end of the day.' And on the golf, in a sentence that is a weather record as much as a sporting one: 'For about six weeks out of the fifty-two rain and wind seriously interfere, but for the rest of the time there is nothing to detract from the full enjoyment of the game.'

Then the apparatus outlived the people who wanted it, and the town took it over. In 1910, at a meeting presided over by the Governor, the management of the course passed to the Colombo-based Ceylon Turf Club, which had the money to improve it. Outside the racing calendar the town library was kept on the ground floor of the grandstand. In 1913 the lake's water was directed into a tunnel to a power station between the town and the railway station, which still supplies the town. Horse racing peaked in the 1950s, was banned outright in 1956, and both this course and the Colombo one closed; the Colombo course became a rugby ground, and when racing returned to the country in 1981 this became the only surviving racecourse in Sri Lanka. In August 2011 ownership passed from the Sri Lanka Turf Club to the Sports Ministry, and the course is now managed by a national sports complex authority with meetings run by the Turf Club. Five meets are held in the April season, and the town still fills for it exactly as Cave described: every room taken, the nine-furlong Governor's Cup run on the Sinhalese and Tamil New Year, golf tournaments, motor hill climbs that have been run since 1934, and a flower show at the end of the month. Then it empties, and for most of the year the plain has the weather to itself.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C004 makes an occasion of wanting a meeting rather than a state. The Pradeepika's sentence is that when a mind meets an agreeable or a neutral object of form or sound, a sticking to that object arises [C004-P:L41], and the Margaya adds the part that matters here: every object carries a good, bad or middling quality, that quality is called the taste of the object, and the greed-rooted mind arises together with the experiencing of the good or the middling one, never with displeasure [C004-M:L15]. So the occasion requires the object to be present and to be met. It cannot be stored.

This history is a hundred and seventy-five years of trying to store it anyway, and it is documented item by item. C005's Margaya lists where such meetings ordinarily happen, and the list is not a paraphrase of this plain, it is an inventory of it: looking at beautiful things for the pleasure of looking, playing games, watching games, preparing pleasing objects among which it names houses, and using them [C005-M:L5], with journeys taken for pleasure in the next line [C005-M:L7]. Cave's 1908 list, written by a man with no interest whatever in Abhidhamma, matches it almost item for item: two lakes, a racecourse, two golf links, clubs with recreation grounds, a trout stream, a public garden, hotels. The sources describe the occasions; the record describes their construction, with dates and the names of the men who signed for them. That is the difference between a film that resembles a concept and a film built on a history that asks the concept's own question.

The specific things that were imported make the point sharper than any argument could. What crossed an ocean was not wealth or power but sensations, itemised: a particular grass, a particular green, a particular breed of cow, three breeds of ram, a horse bred from a named sire, hounds, an oak tree, and a fish that was not in these streams until 1881 and had to be put there by a named official before anybody could have the experience of catching one. The oak in the public garden is the whole film in one object: the first thing planted in a park at six thousand feet in the tropics was a tree from the other side of the world, planted by a visitor, so that the park would feel like somewhere else.

Then the sources provide the brake, and it is the reason this location works rather than merely accuses. C005 sorts by aim and not by act: the same arranging, done from faith, from kindness, or with a plain regard for usefulness, is not counted unwholesome [C005-M:L9]. And the one exemption it spells out at length happens to be the exact subject of this town: clothing prepared and worn in order to remove cold, to remove heat, or to keep off insects is not a fault [C005-M:L17]. The station's own founding reason was medical - Barnes built barracks for invalid soldiers, Baker was sent up as a patient and recovered in a fortnight - so the film cannot even claim that the first motive here was pleasure. The record is complete about what was built and silent about the minds that built it, which is precisely what the sources say a record can be: C004 notes that the same reaching arrives with joy in one person and as a flat neutral feeling in another [C004-M:L17], so no face, no photograph and no archive settles it. The digest's warning about the Pradeepika's own stretch of social commentary [C004-P:L55-L69] - that it is the author's moral argument and would wound if turned into a judgment on a community - is the discipline the whole film runs on, and it is why the colonial history here is recorded and never adjudicated.

Finally, the prompting. The Margaya divides these minds by whether they arise on their own or through a prompting, and says the prompting may come from others or from oneself [C004-M:L21]. What this valley holds is a prompting with nobody left inside it. The rails, the mown grass, the hedges, the grandstand, the oak and the fish are a standing arrangement for contact of a chosen kind, maintained long after everyone who chose it had gone, and taken over by the town that was already here: the grandstand kept the public library on its ground floor, the racing stopped for twenty-five years and started again, the lake became a power supply. The apparatus is permanent and the moment it was built to produce lasts an instant. And the one item on the list that could not be shipped, stocked, fenced or leased is the weather itself. Cave counted it as six bad weeks in fifty-two, which is wrong by the modern normals - in July the plain gets about a fifth of the sunshine it could - and Baker, the man who came for the climate, wrote the finest description of it refusing to cooperate: the mist boiling up from the valleys and sweeping along the surface of the plains, obscuring the view of everything. That is the last shot of the film, and the founder wrote the caption for it in 1848.
what_is_certain: Sir Edward Barnes, fifth Governor of Ceylon, opened the road to the plain and for thirty-six miles beyond it, built barracks and officers' quarters for invalid European troops, and in 1828 built a single-storey holiday residence there, Barnes Hall, at a reported cost of eight thousand pounds. Baker's own book and the modern account of the building that grew into the town's grand hotel give the same figure independently.

Samuel Baker's first visit was in 1847, as a convalescent ordered to the highlands by his doctor after jungle fever, and he stayed a fortnight. This is his own statement in Eight Years' Wanderings in Ceylon (1855): 'Upon my first visit to Newera Ellia, in 1847, Lord Torrington was the governor of Ceylon.'

Baker describes the station as he found it in 1847: 'about twenty private residences, the barracks and officers' quarters, the resthouse and the bazaar; the latter containing about two hundred native inhabitants.' People were living on the plain before the apparatus was built.

Baker's stated aim, in his own words, was to make a residence there 'something approaching to a country life in England, with the advantage of the whole of Ceylon for my manor, and no expense of gamekeepers', and he looked forward 'to establishing a little English village around my own residence'.

Baker bought land from the government at twenty shillings an acre, engaged a bailiff who came with his wife and daughter and nine other emigrants including a blacksmith, and bought farming implements, seeds and saw-mills together with a named list of stock: a half-bred bull (Durham and Hereford), a well-bred Durham cow, three rams (a Southdown, a Leicester and a Cotswold), a thoroughbred entire horse by Charles XII, a small pack of foxhounds and a greyhound called Bran.

The party sailed from London in the Earl of Hardwick in September 1848, Baker having gone ahead by the overland mail in August. The shorthorn cow weighed about thirteen hundredweight; a van built for her collapsed at the first attempt and she walked the hundred and fifteen miles up from the coast with the other animals at ten miles a day.
Baker's own settlement was about two and a half miles from the station, at the eastern end of the plain toward Badulla, chosen because the ground was level enough to plough.

Baker's description of the south-west monsoon on the plain in October 1848: 'the mist boiled up from the valleys and swept along the surface of the plains, obscuring the view of everything, except the pattering rain which descended without ceasing day or night... the dank white lichens hung from the branches of the trees, and the wretchedness of the place was beyond description.'
John Baker, Samuel Baker's brother, is credited with introducing horse racing to the town, having made a training course in the 1840s on a hill near his house for imported English thoroughbreds.

In 1873 Governor Sir William Gregory authorised the damming of the Thalagala stream, which rises on the mountain above the town, in order to make more land available for the town's expansion; the area had been a swampy bog at the foot of the hills. The resulting lake is named after him.

The first race meeting was held in 1875 and was organised by the local Gymkhana Club. Meetings continued intermittently until 1900, when the present course was laid out. Management passed to the Colombo-based Ceylon Turf Club at a meeting in 1910 presided over by the Governor, Sir Henry Edward McCallum.
In 1881 the lake was stocked with trout by C. J. R. Le Mesurier, Assistant Government Agent for the district.

The golf course was constructed in 1889 by a Scottish soldier of the Gordon Highlanders, opened in 1890 with nine holes, acquired a five-room pavilion overlooking the links in 1892 and was extended to eighteen holes in 1893. It covers about forty and a half hectares, is an eighteen-hole par 70 of 5,851 metres, and has over two thousand members.

The public garden had been the research field of the botanical garden at Hakgala; it was formally named in 1897 for Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, and was established with the planting of its first tree, an oak, by a visiting German princess. A river runs through it, forming small lakes.

H. W. Cave's The Book of Ceylon, published in the first decade of the twentieth century, surveys the plain and lists 'two lakes, a racecourse, two golf links, various clubs with their recreation grounds, a well-stocked trout stream, a lovely public garden, several good hotels, fine residences dotting the hill-sides'; states that 'the lake is full of carp, and trout have been successfully introduced into the neighbouring streams, licences to fish in which are granted for any period'; states that the fishing club 'has leased from the Government the fishing rights in all waters at an elevation of over five thousand feet above sea level'; describes the races as the event of the year, with 'All Colombo' flocking up and every bungalow, hotel and club 'taxed to its utmost capacity'; and says of the golf that 'for about six weeks out of the fifty-two rain and wind seriously interfere'.
Outside the racing calendar the town library was kept on the ground floor of the racecourse grandstand.
In 1913 the lake's water was directed into a tunnel feeding a power station between the town and the railway station, which continues to supply the town.

Horse racing in the country peaked in the 1950s, was banned in 1956, and this course and the Colombo course both closed. Racing returned in 1981 and this became the only surviving racecourse in Sri Lanka. In August 2011 ownership passed from the Sri Lanka Turf Club to the Sports Ministry; the course is managed by a national sports complex authority and meetings are run by the Turf Club.

The course has a circumference of about 1,800 metres, roughly nine furlongs, with a 333-metre straight, and is one of the highest racecourses in the world. Five meets are held in the April season, with others in August and December. The nine-furlong Governor's Cup is run on the Sinhalese and Tamil New Year, generally 14 April.
The April season fills the town: accommodation is hard to find, motor hill climbs have been run since 1934, there are golf tournaments, and a flower show is held at the end of the month.

Climate, from the World Meteorological Organization normals for 1991-2020 at the station at 1,894 metres: mean annual temperature 16 degrees; monthly means between 15.1 and 17.4; monthly mean minima between 10.2 and 13.8; record low minus 2.6 in January; annual rainfall 1,838.4 mm across 160.2 rain days of 1 mm or more, with October the wettest month at 246.6 mm. Sunshine and humidity, from a separate German Weather Service series: mean annual humidity 85 per cent, rising to 87 in June and July; recorded sunshine falls to 68.2 hours in July, which is 18 per cent of the possible, 74.4 hours in August (20 per cent) and 84.0 hours in June (23 per cent), against 198.4 hours in March (54 per cent). Frost at night is reported in the coldest months.

The town is the administrative capital of its district, sits at about 1,868 metres below the island's highest mountain, and is a centre of temperate vegetable, flower and dairy farming as well as tea. The nearest railway station is about eight kilometres away.

Fox, deer and elephant hunting are recorded among the pastimes of the colonial station, and a notorious elephant hunter's gravestone is reported to stand in a corner of the golf grounds, not accessible to the public. This is recorded here as a bare fact of the record; none of it is filmed, illustrated or narrated.
what_is_disputed: That Samuel Baker founded the town, and that he did so in 1846. Both are widely repeated, including in the standard encyclopaedia article, and neither is supported by his own book: he gives his first visit as 1847, describes an already-existing station of about twenty houses, a barracks, a rest-house and a bazaar of some two hundred people, and puts his own settlement about two and a half miles away at the other end of the plain. What is defensible is that he is the settlement's most energetic promoter and its most quoted witness. The film does not call him the founder.

The much-quoted phrase that Baker 'imported all the appurtenances of an English country town'. It is attached to him in reference works and in travel writing, but it does not appear anywhere in the full text of Eight Years' Wanderings in Ceylon, which was searched for it. Its source was not located. The phrase is not put in his mouth and is not used; his own wording, 'a little English village' and 'something approaching to a country life in England', is used instead.

That the racecourse was constructed in 1875. 1875 is the date of the first race meeting, organised by the Gymkhana Club; the account of the course itself says meetings ran intermittently until 1900, when the present course was laid out. The two dates are often collapsed into one and the film keeps them apart.

That the Governor's Cup was first contested in 1833. This is stated in the account of the course but predates every other dated element of racing here by more than forty years, including the training course of the 1840s and the first meeting in 1875. It is not used.

The trout. The 1881 stocking of the lake by a named official is dated and firm, but Cave, writing a generation later, says the lake was full of carp while the trout were in the neighbouring streams, so the stocking of the streams is a separate and undated event. The species, whether the fishery survives, who administers it now and whether the streams still hold fish were not established.

Whether any of the dairy farming on this plain today descends from the cattle brought up in 1848. The coincidence is suggestive and nothing was found to support it. It is not claimed anywhere in the film.

The nickname. The place is universally called by a two-word English nickname, which appears as the nickname in the standard encyclopaedia entry, but the date of its first appearance in print and whether it began as a residents' phrase, a planters' phrase or a tourist-board one were not established. The film does not use it in any case, because it is a place name.

The elevation. Sources give 1,868 metres for the town, 1,894 for the meteorological station, 1,902 for a climate database's reference point and 1,830 for the golf course. All are plausible for different points on a plain ringed by hills. The record uses 1,868 for the town and says which figure goes with which source.

The humidity and sunshine figures come from a 1931-1960 or 1961-1990 series rather than from the same 1991-2020 normals as the temperature and rainfall, so the sunshine percentages describe the mid-twentieth-century climate of the station and are treated as indicative rather than current.

Nothing in this record adjudicates the colonial period, and it must not be read as doing so. What is established is what was built, when, and by whom, and what the people who built it said they wanted. The plantation economy of these hills and its labour history are real, are documented elsewhere, are not the subject of this film and are not used here as background colour or as a moral frame.

what_to_film: The racecourse in overcast and drizzle, with nothing happening on it: the flat oval, the white rails, the grandstand empty, and low cloud crossing the whole width of it at standing height. This is the payoff frame and everything else is built around getting it.
The mown grass at close range in the wet: rain standing in beads along the blade tips, a mower's stripe, the seam where mown grass meets rough, boot prints filling with water.

The imported town as architecture rather than as charm: brick, half-timber, chimneys with smoke, clipped hedges along walls, a post office frontage, a church wall, gravel walks and flowerbeds in the public garden, filmed straight on, static, with no warm light and no dressing.
The golf links running up into cloud, filmed from below and from a distance, so that the fairway disappears rather than being displayed.
The dammed lake with the far bank gone into cloud, and the water surface in rain.
Temperature made visible: breath, steam off tea, condensation on the inside of glass, a fire in a grate in the afternoon, wool, a hand round a cup, a heater in a shop doorway.

The working town in the same weather, wide and unsingled: the market under plastic sheeting, the bus stand, milk cans, a van unloading, people walking the lake path in jackets, water being swept off a step.
One matched pair of set-ups filmed twice, once in April with the town full and once in the overcast months with it empty, so that beat six is a cut between identical frames rather than a montage.
A hill stream at water level, long lens, with the fly-fishing water in it; the introduced fish is a fact in the voice and nothing is caught, hooked or landed on camera.
suggested_location.access: By road, on the main highland roads from Kandy through the Ramboda pass or from Badulla and Welimada; the nearest railway station is about eight kilometres away and the town is a long but ordinary drive from any crew base. The town itself, its streets, the public garden, the lake shore and the roads around the racecourse are public. Everything the film actually wants permission for is privately or institutionally held: the racecourse belongs to the state and is managed by a national sports authority with meetings run by the Turf Club, the golf links belong to a members' club with over two thousand members, and the historic hotels and clubs are businesses. Filming on the course outside a meeting, which is what this film needs, is a separate request from filming a meeting, and is the one to make. No permission of any kind has been sought. Drone flight over a municipality and over a lake that has been used as a waterdrome is unverified and may be refused; the treatment is written so the film survives without a drone, and the payoff frame is a ground-level long lens rather than an aerial.
suggested_location.best_time: The overcast months, May to September, and July above all: recorded sunshine at the station falls to about eighteen per cent of the possible in July and twenty in August, and mean humidity reaches eighty-seven per cent in June and July. That is the film. Early morning and the last hour of light for cloud moving at ground level; October and November are the wettest months by rainfall if standing water and heavy drizzle are wanted. January and February for the coldest nights, breath and any chance of frost, accepting brighter days in exchange. April, separately and briefly, for the one matched pair of full-town frames in beat six: the season runs through the Sinhalese and Tamil New Year, with five race meets, golf tournaments and a flower show at the end of the month. A clear blue day is a wasted day on this shoot.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research, and it is unusually well sourced for a colonial subject because the founder wrote a book. Baker's 1847 visit, the state of the station he found, the two hundred people already living in the bazaar, his stated intentions in his own words, the twenty shillings an acre, the emigrants, the itemised livestock, the ship and its sailing date, the cow's van and her walk, the site two and a half miles off, and the October monsoon description are all quoted from the full text of Eight Years' Wanderings in Ceylon (1855) as published by Project Gutenberg, read directly rather than through a secondary summary. The full text was also searched for the phrase about importing the appurtenances of an English country town, which is attached to him everywhere and is not in it; that is recorded as disputed and is not used. The 1908 inventory of the plain, the trout in the streams, the fishing club's lease of all waters above five thousand feet, the description of the race season and the six-bad-weeks-in-fifty-two remark are quoted from the text of H. W. Cave's The Book of Ceylon as digitised at the Internet Archive, also read directly; the OCR of that scan is imperfect and every quoted phrase was read in context, but page numbers were not established and the edition date was not confirmed. The dates for Barnes Hall, the lake, the first race meeting, the 1900 course, the 1881 trout stocking, the golf course, the public garden, the 1910 transfer of management, the 1956 ban, the 1981 return and the 2011 change of ownership come from the encyclopaedia articles listed and were not checked against printed originals; where they disagree with Baker's own account, or with each other, the disagreement is recorded in what_is_disputed and is not resolved. The climate figures are from the World Meteorological Organization 1991-2020 normals for the station at 1,894 metres for temperature and rainfall, and from a separate German Weather Service series for humidity and sunshine, which is why the sunshine percentages are treated as indicative rather than current. Coordinates are the encyclopaedia's for the town centre; the lake and the public garden have their own published coordinates a little to the south-east and north respectively, and the racecourse coordinate was not separately established. Nothing has been verified on the ground: no permission, no access, no drone clearance, no confirmation that the months named actually deliver cloud at grass level over the course, and no check on the present state of the trout streams. The record of colonial hunting on this station is noted as a bare fact and nothing in the film uses it. The demographic composition of the town is documented and is deliberately left out of this record, because the film does not narrate anybody's class or ethnicity.

unknowns: No access, permission or clearance of any kind has been sought. Filming inside the racecourse, the golf links, the clubs and the historic hotels would each need a separate permission from a separate body, none of which has been approached.
Drone permission over a municipal area, and over a lake listed as a waterdrome, is unverified and may be refused. The treatment is written so that the film survives without a drone.
Whether the modern dairy industry on this plain descends in any way from the cattle brought up in 1848 is unverified and is not claimed anywhere in the film.
The current state of the introduced trout fishery, who administers it and whether the streams still hold fish, is desk research only.

Nothing has been checked on the ground: which months actually deliver cloud at grass level over the course, whether the grandstand and rails are as photographed, and whether the April and off-season material can be matched frame for frame.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Claude's suggestion and awaits Chathura's verdict; its supporting detail is desk research and is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
